ground_truth.title: Best EVs of 2026
ground_truth.author: John Goreham
ground_truth.main_content:
The Ford Mustang Mach-E Rally earns Car Talk’s top pick for EVs. Image by John Goreham

Heading into 2026, the U.S. EV market has boiled down to a two-car parade: Tesla’s Model 3 and Model Y. Together, they command roughly the same market share as the other 68 electric models combined. Calling that “dominance” barely covers it.
Elsewhere, the landscape looks like a dealership after a clearance sale. Ford has pulled the plug on the F-150 Lightning. The Tesla Cybertruck has landed with a thud. VW, Nissan, Acura, and Chevrolet have quietly shuffled their underperforming EVs off the lot. And brands like RAM, Kia, and Jeep have eased off the accelerator, hitting pause on once-ambitious EV launch plans.

Electric vehicles have hit a few potholes lately, with U.S. market share slipping back to roughly 2022 levels as we head into 2026. That doesn’t mean there aren’t outstanding EVs for the right buyer to choose from. Many automakers are now on their fourth generation of EVs, producing new EVs that don’t make yesterday’s mistakes. The 2026 crop charges faster, plugs in more conveniently, and travels far enough that range anxiety is starting to feel a bit more like “I think I forgot to buy toothpaste,” than “I think I left the stove on.”

At Car Talk, we award what we test, so the winners on our list are all vehicles our testing staff have driven for a week or more. Our impressions are our own, not what the manufacturers tell us their EVs will be like some fine day. That said, there are two models that we have not been able to test, which we will mention, since they are new generations of EVs we would have awarded even in their old versions. Those are the 2027 Chevrolet Bolt arriving at dealers as this story is written, and the 2026 Nissan Leaf, which has already begun its customer deliveries.

Why You Can Trust Car Talk

Car Talk has been poking, prodding, and road-testing EVs since 2010, back when the Nissan Leaf quietly ushered in the modern electric era. Since then, we’ve driven just about every EV sold in America, save for a few oddballs hiding in the margins.

Our test team spans mechanics, engineers, and veteran vehicle testers with decades of grease, graphs, and miles under their belts. They all had a hand in shaping this list, even if there’s only one name at the top of the page.

Car Talk has staff members who own EVs and use them as daily drivers, and we have testers with as many as four EV chargers at home. We also test and review home and public chargers, so we know our kWs from our KWhs. That said, we learn more every day, and we will be the first to request help from any source that offers it. As we often say here at Car Talk, “Our Humility Is What Makes Us Great!”

Among EV owners, drivers, and true believers, there’s a long-running argument about whether plug-in hybrids deserve the EV badge. Some say yes. Others clutch their charging cables and say, "Absolutely not."

Here at Car Talk, we run a big tent. That means including a few of the best plug-in hybrids alongside pure EVs. If you don’t agree, feel free to skip that section. Or send us a strongly worded email. We’ll take it as proof that we’re being inclusive.

Best EVs of 2026

Best EV Overall - Ford Mustang Mach-E Rally

Best Affordable EV - 2026 Nissan Leaf and 2027 Chevrolet Bolt

Best Luxury EV - Genesis GV60

Best Battery-Electric Hatchback “Sedan” - Kia EV6

Best Performance EV - Hyundai Ioniq 5 N

Most Reliable EV - Ford Mustang Mach-E

Best EV Truck - Chevrolet Silverado EV and GMC Sierra EV

Best Off-Roader EV - GMC Hummer

Best Plug-In Hybrid-Electric SUV: Toyota RAV4 Prime Plug-in Hybrid

Best Supercar With a Plug - McLaren Artura Spider PHEV

Best Newly-Released EVs: 2026 Nissan Leaf and 2027 Chevrolet Bolt

Nissan Leaf

The Nissan Leaf is a vehicle we’ve loved since its second generation. The Leaf has never been out of production and has been on sale in America now longer than any other plug-in model. We’ll be frank; The thing we love most about the Leaf is that it is affordable. Out the door, consumer costs for new Leafs are around $30K. As we type this story in our PJs right now, it is the only EV in America that can make that claim. During 2025, the outgoing Leaf generation had insane lease deals. Multiple colleagues of ours leased new Leafs in Colorado for under $25 per month. That’s not a typo. Twenty-five bucks. That’s the cost of a latte per week to drive a brand-new car. Colorado offered nutty rebates, and the federal tax incentives were still in effect. We doubt we’ll see those deals again, but who knows? For 2026, the all-new Leaf has a completely new powertrain with much more range, and the crazy CHAdeMO charge port is gone for good. We’ll edit our story later after our staff has had the opportunity to test the Leaf, but we wanted to put the most affordable EV in America at the very top of our list.

Chevrolet Bolt

The only reason the Chevy Bolt lost its top spot on our Best EVs list is that Chevy stopped making them. We’ve driven Bolts all over the inner city of Boston, up mountains using the ample torque to claw for traction, then down mountains using only regenerative braking, stuffing electrons back into the battery in a very satisfying way. We’ve worn the tires down on lonely back-country roads on long touring trips. We’ve driven Bolts hands-free for miles on the highway using GM’s brilliant Super Cruise assisted driving system. Every journey was a joy. We liked the base Bolts very much and downright LOVED the Bolt EUV. Then, like the Volt before it, GM pulled the car off the market. Facepalm.

Now the Bolt is back! It’s all-new for 2026 and will carry a 2027 model year nameplate. It has a smidge more range, it’s a smidge bigger, its already great looks are now a bit classier and refined. Early indications are that it will be neck-and-neck with the Leaf for the most affordable EV in America. There is just one small detail that has us up at night, worried about this great car’s future at the top of our list. GM has pulled Android Auto and Apple CarPlay and will instead offer a system that is free to start, but requires a subscription down the road to work. Boo! A colleague we consider the most tech-savvy in the nation tested this infotainment system and created a 30-minute “why I despise this system” video that has become legendary among testers. We’ll hold our fire until we test the car and comment on it as a whole.

Car Talk’s GM electric vehicle expert and owner, Zane Merva, suggested that the Bolt should be a big success for GM, saying, “All the signs point to the Bolt being a smash hit once again, and its deliveries will likely be limited only by GM’s production volume.” He went on to add, “Would I like Apple CarPlay? Sure, but it’s just one aspect of a vehicle.”

Best EV Overall: Ford Mustang Mach-E Rally

When the Ford Mustang Mach-E launched, we were among the first publications to test it for a week. We immediately drove it to a Tesla dealership and back-to-backed it against the Tesla Model Y. Based on our first-hand experience, the Mach-E was the better choice. Better infotainment, better interior, better ride, better styling, better dealer network, and equal performance. However, there were a few rough edges for Ford to smooth over.

This past fall, we tested the Mach-E for the fourth time, this time in its Rally trim. We’ve tested mid-trims and top trims. The Rally has over 700 lb-ft of torque. This thing rips! Car Talk’s John Paul said, “There is Mustang DNA in this car.” All the great core features are there, plus about 300 lb-ft of torque more than you will ever need, but you will enjoy having.

The nifty feature that won our hearts was Michelin CrossClimate2 all-weather, severe-snow-duty-rated tires straight from the factory! We don’t hide the fact that we all have a pretty serious tire fetish here at Car Talk. We test as many as six tire models at a time on our Car Talk family fleet, and the tire that we would call “the most important tire of the decade” is this Michelin CrossClimate2. Car Talk’s expert tester, John Paul, said, “The Mach-E with AWD and winter-capable tires is a great New England vehicle, stable and sure-footed.” No need for winter tires, and no downsides to the added cold-weather traction. There are many great EVs to choose from in 2026. This attention to detail by Ford’s team was a deciding factor that moved the Mach-E Rally from being a segment winner to our number one spot overall. What helped secure the win was Mach-E earning the highest reliability scores for the last two consecutive years among EVs.

Best Battery-Electric Hatchback Sedan: Kia EV6

Most of the EVs we test are hatchbacks we’d also term crossovers. There are many fantastic ones, notably our Best EV Overall pick from last year, the Hyundai Ioniq 5. Kia marches to the beat of its own drummer and bucked the trend by making its best EV crossover look a lot like a sedan.

Our expert mechanic and vehicle tester, Jr. Damato, insisted the Kia EV6 be included on this list of Best EVs, and he didn’t have to lobby hard. John Paul, Zane Merva, and I already had it on our own short list of best EVs. The only question was which category it would land in. Jr. called the EV6 “Fast, fun, and easy on the eyes.” If you’re looking for a roomy five-passenger sedan-like EV, start with the EV6 from Kia. If you prefer a more traditional five-door hatchback design, or top pick from 2025, the Hyundai Ioniq 5 is an outstanding EV.

Best Plug-In Hybrid-Electric SUV: Toyota RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid

If you need an EV that covers all your normal driving in full-electric mode and also delivers over 600 miles of uninterrupted driving as a hybrid, look no further than the Toyota RAV4 PHEV. About to enter its sixth generation as a crossover, and its second as a plug-in hybrid-electric vehicle, the RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid (formerly the RAV4 Prime) is a standout in its segment.

The RAV4 is the top-selling personal-use vehicle model in America. Yes, it outsells the Model Y. For 2026, every RAV trim will be able to temporarily drive in all-electric mode. The RAV4 Plug-in can do so for 50 miles. The biggest news is that the RAV4 Plug-in will also be able to DC charge in 2026. With features like a built-in dash-cam, well over 300 hp, and a spare tire, Toyota continues to up the ante in the crossover segment.

We’ve awarded the RAV4 plug-in hybrid every year we’ve published this list, and the outgoing 2025 RAV4 would have beaten every other plug-in on this list. Our 2026 Model Year RAV4 Plug-in test is scheduled for late Q1. Watch for updates here.

Best Low-Cost EV: 2026 Nissan Leaf

As we mentioned at the start of our story, the new Leaf beat the new Chevy Bolt to market by many months. With a starting consumer cost well below $30K, the Leaf is the easy winner of this segment. The new Leaf will match the Bolt’s range with its base trim and offers a higher trim with over 300 miles of range. The new Leaf abandons the ridiculous Euro-spec DC charging standard it has had for the past 15 years in 2026 and will boast dual J1772 and NACS charging ports. If shoppers are not beating down the doors of Nissan’s dealers to buy the new Leaf, we will be surprised. We would have placed the outgoing Leaf on this list of Best EVs in the low-cost category, so we feel that the new one should be mentioned as well, even though Nissan hasn’t found one to send to us yet.

Best Supercar With a Plug: McLaren Artura Spider PHEV

So, you want a supercar that can drive around town on electricity alone. However, you are not quite ready to give up the experience of a thrilling liquid-fueled engine? McLaren has exactly what you are looking for. The Artura Spider is all things in one. It’s an EV for up to around 30 miles, it’s an ultra-high-performance supercar, and it’s also a convertible. We had the pleasure of driving this vehicle for a week, and it quickly reset our gauge as to what “Best” can really mean.

Best Luxury EV: Genesis GV60

The Genesis GV60 is now a multi-year winner at Car Talk. This luxury EV delivers tremendous performance, true luxury, and a battery-electric powertrain that offers among the fastest charging you can buy. For 2026, Genesis makes many small tweaks to the styling and interior. Pair the outstanding car with a warranty and ownership experience that is at the very top of the industry, and you have the makings for a segment win for Genesis. Car Talk expert, John Paul, lobbied for a slightly larger Genesis GV as Best Luxury EV title, saying, “My top EV pick would be the Genesis GV70.” If you need a bit more space than the GV60 offers, Genesis has you covered.

Best EV Truck: Tie Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra

Zane Merva’s close connections to GM’s truck world scored our team some test drives we would otherwise not have gotten. Zane was also among the first owners of a GM electric truck. He breaks down the three GM EVs this way: the best pickups are the GMC Sierra EV and the Chevrolet Silverado EV. The best off-roader is the GMC Hummer, available as an SUV or a truck.

“With 450+ miles of range, a folding mid-gate, and more outlets than your garage, the Silverado and Sierra EVs are refined powerhouses,” Zane says. “You get industry-best infotainment, 4-wheel steering, and nearly 700 hp from a battery that can also power your home for a week.” Zane is a longtime tester of all-terrain off-roaders, which he often tows to trailheads in Rural New Hampshire. He told Car Talk, “While gas owners hesitate, EV owners know the Silverado and Sierra EVs tow better than a 3500HD."

Best Off-Roader EV: GMC Hummer

"With 1,000 hp, 35-inch tires, and axles the size of your wrist, the HUMMER EV is virtually unstoppable,” says Zane Merva. “GM’s electronic torque vectoring makes technical off-roading 'point and shoot,' while a 3-second 0-60 dominates the pavement - Oh, and it Crabwalks.” Zane has been off-road and off-pavement in virtually every vehicle in the segment and tells us that the Hummer isn’t just the best “EV off-roader.” It’s the best period. He does have one thing to add, however. “The downside is the Hummer has the aerodynamics of a brick, so highway driving to your favorite trail drains the battery fast."

Best Performance EV: Hyundai Ioniq 5 N

Hyundai went to great lengths to differentiate its Ioniq 5 N from the rest of the great Ioniq 5 trims. This trim features special drive modes that let you drift the vehicle and launch it like a cannonball. It has a racecar suspension, racecar brakes, racecar tires, and even a seat that looks perfect for track days. Hyundai made all the right moves with this battery-electric performance vehicle. For 2026, expect the N to switch to an NACS charging port, which the rest of the Ioniq 5 line already had last year. Zane Merva commented on this segment win, saying, “There are a surprising number of performance EVs in 2026, but it’s hard to top the Ioniq 5 N.”

Most Reliable EV: Ford Mustang Mach-E

We looked at Consumer Reports Reliability results for battery-electric vehicles and found that the Mustang Mach-E scored above 80 in 2024, and over 90/100 in 2025, the last year for which data is available. By contrast, the Tesla Model Y and the Hyundai Ioniq 5 both scored in the 30s/100 range for 2025.

How Much Range Do EVs Offer?

Heading into 2026, EV range varies from about 250 miles at the low end to about 450 miles at the high end. Having tested a wide variety of EVs, we can tell you that 50 miles of range, one way or the other, really isn't all that important. An EV with 275 miles of range won’t be much different than one with 325 miles. What matters most is having a Level 2 charger at home and being able to use the Tesla Supercharger Network. Without both of these on our side, we would never even consider a battery-electric vehicle. Here are some highly-rated EVs and the ranges they offer.

Plug-in Hybrid-Electric Model EV only Range Range when full of gas and fully charged

Are EVs Safe? Which Are Safest?

EVs consistently score highly in IIHS and NHTSA crash testing. For example, the Ford Mustang Mach-E earns the highest possible safety rating, the IIHS Top Safety Pick+ designation. EVs are generally heavier than conventional vehicles in their size segment, and weight is a plus in a multi-car crash. EVs also have the weight down low, which helps with stability.

Should I Buy an EV?

Nope. But you should lease one if an EV fits your lifestyle. Manufacturers have structured the best EV deals as leases. If you are an everyday driver, this will be the best way to own one. It shields you from depreciation, or at least makes it work in your favor. It means you will never own the vehicle outside the warranty, so any hiccups won't cost you any money.

Based on our decades of testing EVs, we would suggest that if you cannot charge at your residence using a Level 2 charger of your own, don’t own a battery-electric vehicle (battery-only). Public charging is improving dramatically, but it is for road trips and emergencies, not for daily charging. If you can charge on a Level 2 charger at work, consider an EV seriously, but not if you need to share it there.

There is a long list of great green vehicles with and without plugs that folks without a home charger can buy. We’d look at those.

How Much Do EVs Cost?

Heading into 2026, two models of battery-electric vehicles will be priced under $30K in base trims. Those are the 2026 Nissan Leaf and the 2027 Chevy Bolt. The sky is the limit at the very high end of the market, with some Porsche models costing as much as $200,000 in top trims. The plug-in hybrid-electric McLaren Artura Spider starts near $300K and can rise quite a bit if you check off a lot of boxes. For the most part, EVs like the Tesla Model Y, Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Mustang Mach-E have prices in the $40K to $70K range. The Toyota RAV4 Plug-in will sell for about $50K. The vast majority of EV owners lease them, rather than buy them outright. Hyundai’s CEO told us last year that it is roughly 80% lease for that brand’s EVs.

EV Model Award Starting Price At Time Of Publication

How Many People Can Fit in an EV?

EVs tend to be very roomy due to their flat-floor design. Among the smallest battery-electric vehicles sold today is the 2027 Chevy Bolt. It will seat two comfortably, four if you need it to, and five in a pinch. The Mustang Mach-E is roomy in the front and back for four and can seat five just fine. Hyundai and Kia both have three-row EV SUVs. The GMC and Chevrolet EV trucks are HUGE inside and can easily seat five comfortably. The McLaren Artura Spider on our list is a two-seat plug-in coupe/convertible, and it’s very roomy for each of its two passengers for a sports car.

What Features Should I Look For in an EV?

Heading into 2026, a key change for Evs is that most will now have an NACS charger port. We’d consider this an important feature and be hesitant to buy an EV without it. Also, we’d be sure the peak DC charging rate is above 150 kW. Higher is better. If you are buying a daily driver, we would consider a spare tire, self-sealing tires, or run-flat tires to be a big plus. Otherwise, you are at risk if a tire is damaged. Finally, we are big fans of Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. These offer the best in-vehicle experience and are free to owners who choose to use them. We would caution shoppers not to fall in love with an EV before they know whether this much-loved infotainment technology is included.

How Did EVs Overtake Combustion Engine Cars In the Performance World?

Battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles have started from the top-down to overtake performance segments one by one. It’s hard to find a gas vehicle that can accelerate as hard and as fast as most EVs in most segments. With instant, abundant torque, the only real question is whether the EV can put the power down.

For a while, plug-ins were one-trick ponies and only had the edge off the line. However, the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, Dodge Charger Daytona, Tesla Model 3 Performance, and many other EVs are now legitimate muscle cars, sports cars, and performance cars. The McLaren Artura Spider is a flat-out supercar, and the highest-performance Corvette is also going plug-in.

About the expert

Zane Merva

Zane is also our expert on gas and electric pickups, detailing and towing. He’s no stranger to towing all-terrain vehicles (ATVs) to trailheads for testing. Zane has a background in technology, holding both an Associate of Science (A.S.) and a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree. These led him to pass on that knowledge as an educator at a tech school. Finally, Zane has 15 years of experience... See full bio

FAQ

Car Talk named the Ford Mustang Mach-E the best EV overall and the Nissan Leaf the best affordable EV in a recent story.

Battery-electric vehicles like the Ford Mustang Mach-E earn top safety scores.

Tesla owns roughly 50% of the U.S. EV market with the Model Y and Model 3 alone. It’s fair to say Tesla is among the best EV makers on the planet. Car Talk would add Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, Nissan, and Kia to the list.

The Ford Mustang Mach-E. Consumer Reports data shows that Tesla did not earn the highest scores in the last full year of its survey (2025).

Heading into 2026, most top-selling EVs have a range of roughly 250 to 325 miles. Look carefully when shopping. The range of a model varies by trim, and the longest-range trim is not always the best trim overall. Some EVs, like GM’s high-priced trucks, now approach 500 miles in some top trims.

John Paul, Zane Merva, and I already had it on our own short list of best EVs. The only question was which category it would land in. Jr. called the EV6 “Fast, fun, and easy on the eyes.” If you’re looking for a roomy five-passenger sedan-like EV, start with the EV6 from Kia. If you prefer a more traditional five-door hatchback design, or top pick from 2025, the Hyundai Ioniq 5 is an outstanding EV.

## Best Plug-In Hybrid-Electric SUV: Toyota RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid

If you need an EV that covers all your normal driving in full-electric mode and also delivers over 600 miles of uninterrupted driving as a hybrid, look no further than the Toyota RAV4 PHEV. About to enter its sixth generation as a crossover, and its second as a plug-in hybrid-electric vehicle, the RAV4 Plug-in Hybrid (formerly the RAV4 Prime) is a standout in its segment.

The RAV4 is the top-selling personal-use vehicle model in America. Yes, it outsells the Model Y. For 2026, every RAV trim will be able to temporarily drive in all-electric mode. The RAV4 Plug-in can do so for 50 miles. The biggest news is that the RAV4 Plug-in will also be able to DC charge in 2026. With features like a built-in dash-cam, well over 300 hp, and a spare tire, Toyota continues to up the ante in the crossover segment.

We’ve awarded the RAV4 plug-in hybrid every year we’ve published this list, and the outgoing 2025 RAV4 would have beaten every other plug-in on this list. Our 2026 Model Year RAV4 Plug-in test is scheduled for late Q1. Watch for updates here.

As we mentioned at the start of our story, the new Leaf beat the new Chevy Bolt to market by many months. With a starting consumer cost well below $30K, the Leaf is the easy winner of this segment. ## How Much Range Do EVs Offer?

Heading into 2026, EV range varies from about 250 miles at the low end to about 450 miles at the high end. Having tested a wide variety of EVs, we can tell you that 50 miles of range, one way or the other, really isn't all that important. An EV with 275 miles of range won’t be much different than one with 325 miles. What matters most is having a Level 2 charger at home and being able to use the Tesla Supercharger Network. ## Are EVs Safe? Which Are Safest?

EVs consistently score highly in IIHS and NHTSA crash testing. For example, the Ford Mustang Mach-E earns the highest possible safety rating, the IIHS Top Safety Pick+ designation. EVs are generally heavier than conventional vehicles in their size segment, and weight is a plus in a multi-car crash. EVs also have the weight down low, which helps with stability.

## Should I Buy an EV?

Nope. But you should lease one if an EV fits your lifestyle. Manufacturers have structured the best EV deals as leases. If you are an everyday driver, this will be the best way to own one. It shields you from depreciation, or at least makes it work in your favor. It means you will never own the vehicle outside the warranty, so any hiccups won't cost you any money.

Based on our decades of testing EVs, we would suggest that if you cannot charge at your residence using a Level 2 charger of your own, don’t own a battery-electric vehicle (battery-only). Public charging is improving dramatically, but it is for road trips and emergencies, not for daily charging. If you can charge on a Level 2 charger at work, consider an EV seriously, but not if you need to share it there.

There is a long list of great green vehicles with and without plugs that folks without a home charger can buy. We’d look at those.

## How Much Do EVs Cost?

Heading into 2026, two models of battery-electric vehicles will be priced under $30K in base trims. Those are the 2026 Nissan Leaf and the 2027 Chevy Bolt. The sky is the limit at the very high end of the market, with some Porsche models costing as much as $200,000 in top trims. The plug-in hybrid-electric McLaren Artura Spider starts near $300K and can rise quite a bit if you check off a lot of boxes. For the most part, EVs like the Tesla Model Y, Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Mustang Mach-E have prices in the $40K to $70K range. The Toyota RAV4 Plug-in will sell for about $50K. The vast majority of EV owners lease them, rather than buy them outright. Hyundai’s CEO told us last year that it is roughly 80% lease for that brand’s EVs.

## How Many People Can Fit in an EV?

EVs tend to be very roomy due to their flat-floor design. Among the smallest battery-electric vehicles sold today is the 2027 Chevy Bolt. It will seat two comfortably, four if you need it to, and five in a pinch. The Mustang Mach-E is roomy in the front and back for four and can seat five just fine. Hyundai and Kia both have three-row EV SUVs. The GMC and Chevrolet EV trucks are HUGE inside and can easily seat five comfortably. The McLaren Artura Spider on our list is a two-seat plug-in coupe/convertible, and it’s very roomy for each of its two passengers for a sports car.

## What Features Should I Look For in an EV?

Heading into 2026, a key change for Evs is that most will now have an NACS charger port. We’d consider this an important feature and be hesitant to buy an EV without it. Also, we’d be sure the peak DC charging rate is above 150 kW. Higher is better. If you are buying a daily driver, we would consider a spare tire, self-sealing tires, or run-flat tires to be a big plus. Otherwise, you are at risk if a tire is damaged. Finally, we are big fans of Apple CarPlay and Android Auto. These offer the best in-vehicle experience and are free to owners who choose to use them. We would caution shoppers not to fall in love with an EV before they know whether this much-loved infotainment technology is included.

## How Did EVs Overtake Combustion Engine Cars In the Performance World?

Battery-electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles have started from the top-down to overtake performance segments one by one. It’s hard to find a gas vehicle that can accelerate as hard and as fast as most EVs in most segments. With instant, abundant torque, the only real question is whether the EV can put the power down.

For a while, plug-ins were one-trick ponies and only had the edge off the line. However, the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, Dodge Charger Daytona, Tesla Model 3 Performance, and many other EVs are now legitimate muscle cars, sports cars, and performance cars. The McLaren Artura Spider is a flat-out supercar, and the highest-performance Corvette is also going plug-in.
